power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is an important predictive biomarker for poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) therapy in ovarian cancer (OC).
However, real-world data on HRD prevalence and assay performance in Indian patients are limited.
This study evaluated commercial HRD assays, then developed an in-house HRD assay and characterized HRD and BRCA alterations in a large real-world Indian OC cohort.
Methods: This retrospective study included 4,163 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) OC samples tested between 2021 and 2025.
HRD and BRCA status were initially assessed using the AmoyDx HRD Focus Panel (n=1,097) and SOPHiA DDM HRD Solution (n=470).

Subsequently, 170 representative samples were used for the development and validation of an in-house HRD assay (MG_HRD), with external concordance assessed using the Myriad myChoice CDx assay in a subset of samples.
Following validation, MG_HRD was implemented in routine clinical practice and applied to an independent cohort of 2,596 OC samples.
HRD prevalence, BRCA mutation status, and clinicopathological associations were evaluated in all cohorts.
Results: Among 4,163 ovarian cancer samples, HRD positivity was observed in 52.4% of cases, and pathogenic/likely pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants were identified in 23.6% of cases.
Notably, 28.8% of tumors were BRCA wild-type but HRD-positive.
BRCA-mutated tumors demonstrated significantly higher HRD genomic instability scores than BRCA wild-type tumors (p<0.001).
text.formatted: BRCA-mutated tumors demonstrated significantly higher HRD genomic instability scores than BRCA wild-type tumors (p<0.001).

text.text: HRD positivity was significantly enriched in high grade serous ovarian carcinomas.
Remarkably, the BRCA1 c.68_69del (p.Glu23ValfsTer17) founder mutation was detected in 14.2% (97/685) of cases among the pathogenic variants in our study.

The MG_HRD assay showed excellent concordance with commercial assays, achieving 97.1% overall agreement, 98.3% negative percent agreement (NPA), and 96.4% positive percent agreement (PPA), with complete concordance observed in the externally evaluated Myriad subset.
Conclusions: This is the first Indian study to develop, validate, and implement an in-house HRD assay and evaluate HRD across three testing platforms in a large real-world OC cohort.

The high prevalence of BRCA wild-type/HRD-positive tumors highlight the importance of comprehensive HRD testing, whereas the strong performance of MG_HRD supports its use as a reliable and cost-effective alternative for routine clinical practice.

Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is a significant genomic instability phenotype resulting from impaired repair of DNA double-strand breaks through the homologous recombination repair (HRR) pathway 1 .
text.formatted: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is a significant genomic instability phenotype resulting from impaired repair of DNA double-strand breaks through the homologous recombination repair (HRR) pathway <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: This deficiency results in the accumulation of genomic scars, including loss of heterozygosity (LOH), telomeric allelic imbalance (TAI), and large-scale state transitions (LST), which together contribute to tumorigenesis 2 .
HRD is highly prevalent in ovarian cancer (OC), particularly in high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), which is a common histological subtype, comprising 70% of OC cases 2, 3 .
text.formatted: HRD is highly prevalent in ovarian cancer (OC), particularly in high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), which is a common histological subtype, comprising 70% of OC cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: HRD has become an important predictive biomarker for response to platinum-based chemotherapy and poly (ADPribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) in OC.
PARPi functions through the principle of synthetic lethality, where the inhibition of single-strand DNA repair results in the accumulation of DNA damage, which is lethal in HR-deficient tumors 4.
text.formatted: PARPi functions through the principle of synthetic lethality, where the inhibition of single-strand DNA repair results in the accumulation of DNA damage, which is lethal in HR-deficient tumors <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref>.

text.text: Approximately 50% of HGSC cases exhibit HRD, either due to pathogenic BRCA1/2 mutations [BRCA1/2_mut], which constitutes approximately 20-25% or through genomic scar markers such as LOH, TAI, and LST 3 .

text.text: The HRD genomic scar score is calculated based on the quantification of these genomic scars 1 .

text.text: While BRCA1/2 mutation testing remains a cornerstone of molecular diagnostics, it is increasingly recognized that a significant proportion of HRDpositive tumors are BRCA1/2 wild-type (BRCA1/2_wt).
This highlights the need for comprehensive testing strategies that integrate both BRCA1/2 mutation analysis and genomic scar score-based HRD assessment 5 .

text.text: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) technology plays a crucial role in identifying patients for targeted therapeutics by enabling comprehensive analysis of the genomic scars and molecular alterations that drive ovarian cancer 6.

text.text: Several commercial and laboratory-developed NGS-based assays are currently available for HRD testing.
Among these, the Myriad MyChoice CDx assay (Myriad Genetics, Salt Lake City, UT, USA) is a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved companion diagnostic HRD assay for PARP inhibitor therapy.

This assay integrates BRCA1/2 mutation status with a genomic instability score (GIS) derived from the combined score of LOH, TAI, and LST, with a predefined cutoff of ≥42 to define HRD positivity 7, 8 .
text.formatted: This assay integrates BRCA1/2 mutation status with a genomic instability score (GIS) derived from the combined score of LOH, TAI, and LST, with a predefined cutoff of ≥42 to define HRD positivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: Despite its clear predictive value, the widespread adoption of this assay faces challenges because of its high cost, long turnaround time, and limited accessibility due to centralized testing 6.
text.formatted: Despite its clear predictive value, the widespread adoption of this assay faces challenges because of its high cost, long turnaround time, and limited accessibility due to centralized testing <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref>.

text.text: To overcome the limitations of the Myriad MyChoice CDx assay, several alternative commercial HRD diagnostic assays have been developed, including the AmoyDx HRD Focus Panel, SOPHiA DDM HRD Solution, FoundationOne CDx, Leuven HRD, and SeqOne HRD assays.

Although these platforms are designed with the common objective of determining HRD status, they differ considerably in assay design, including gene content, single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) backbone, sequencing methodologies and bioinformatic algorithms 7, 9, 10.
text.formatted: Although these platforms are designed with the common objective of determining HRD status, they differ considerably in assay design, including gene content, single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) backbone, sequencing methodologies and bioinformatic algorithms <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref>.

text.text: The lack of harmonized methodologies highlights the need for scalable, reproducible, and locally deployable diagnostic solutions for HRD assessment in ovarian cancer 3, 6 .
text.formatted: The lack of harmonized methodologies highlights the need for scalable, reproducible, and locally deployable diagnostic solutions for HRD assessment in ovarian cancer <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Each of these HRD assays uses different genomic instability metrics and positivity thresholds for HRD classification 7 .
text.formatted: Each of these HRD assays uses different genomic instability metrics and positivity thresholds for HRD classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: For example, the AmoyDx HRD Focus Panel uses a Genomic Scar Score (GSS) threshold of ≥50; the SOPHiA DDM HRD Solution applies a Genomic Integrity Index (GII) threshold of ≥0; FoundationOne CDx primarily relies on genomic loss of heterozygosity (gLOH) with a cutoff of ≥16; Leuven HRD employs a GIS derived from combined genomic scar markers with a cutoff of >56; and SeqOne HRD uses a proprietary genomic instability threshold 7 .

text.text: Among these commercial decentralized NGS-based assays, AmoyDx and SOPHiA provide the most practical and reliable alternatives by enabling in-house HRD assessment using standardized analytical workflows.
Their high concordance with established reference assays supports their implementation in routine clinical HRD testing [10] [11] [12] [13] .
text.formatted: Their high concordance with established reference assays supports their implementation in routine clinical HRD testing <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> .

text.text: Therefore, in this study, we chose to perform these two commercial assays in our MedGenome laboratory along with our in-house developed HRD assay, designated as the MedGenome HRD (MG_HRD) assay, to evaluate the HRD status in OC samples.
In this retrospective study, we validated the analytical performance and feasibility of the MG_HRD assay by comparing it with two commercially available HRD assays: AmoyDx and SOPHiA.
A limited subset of samples underwent external benchmarking using the Myriad myChoice CDx assay.
As mentioned above, the HRD metrics of all these assays are different.
Hence, to ensure consistency across platforms, these metrics were collectively referred to as the HRD genomic score (HRD_GS) in this study.
The primary objectives of this study were to assess cross-platform agreement using concordance metrics and to evaluate the analytical performance of the MG_HRD assay.
The secondary objectives were to determine the prevalence of HRD, alterations in BRCA1/2, and the status of HRD_GS across the three assays.
Furthermore, we investigated the association between HRD status with tumor content, and histological subtypes across a large, independent ovarian cancer cohort for all three assays.
Through this comprehensive evaluation, we aimed to investigate the applicability and scalability of MG_HRD testing for the molecular diagnosis of ovarian cancer.

text.text: In this study, a large independent clinical cohort of 4163 patients with OC was analyzed for HRD testing using three distinct assays.

Among these, 1097 patients (26.4%) were assessed using the AmoyDx (assay 1), 470 patients (11.3%) using the SOPHiA (assay 2), and 2596 patients (62.4%) using the MG_HRD (assay 3).
A small subset of samples was analyzed using the SOPHiA assay (n = 14), which yielded inconclusive HRD results.
Therefore, these samples were excluded from downstream analysis, resulting in 470 evaluable samples for the SOPHiA assay [Figure 1A].

text.text: To enable HRD assessment using our indigenous assay, we designed a custom panel with dual functionality: (a) genome-wide detection of copy number alterations using strategically distributed SNP markers, (b) identification of pathogenic variants in BRCA1/2 and other homologous recombination repair (HRR) genes.

The panel incorporates genome-wide SNP biallelic markers selected to ensure broad representation across diverse ethnic populations, together with a targeted gene panel comprising key HRR-associated genes and CCNE1.
The targeted panel includes 17 genes: ATM, BARD1, BRCA1, BRCA2, BRIP1, CDK12, CHEK1, CHEK2, FANCL, FGFR1, PALB2, PPP2R2A, RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D, RAD54L, and

The genome-wide SNP backbone was selected from well-curated population reference databases, including the 1000 Genomes Project, GenomeAsia, gnomAD, and our internally curated SAS-ATLAS database, which comprises data from over 100000 samples.
SNP selection was performed by adapting the methodology described by Timms et al 16 .
text.formatted: SNP selection was performed by adapting the methodology described by Timms et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: Briefly, candidate SNPs were filtered to retain markers with a minor allele frequency (MAF) greater than 5%, low linkage disequilibrium and exclusion from regions associated with segmental duplications, problematic genomic regions, repetitive elements and low-mappability sequences.
Using this strategy, approximately 46,000 genome-wide SNP markers were prioritized for panel design.
The shortlisted SNPs were subsequently evaluated for probe design, and the optimal probes were selected based on simulated hybridization performance.
The probes for both SNPs and HRR targets were densely and differentially tiled (3X-10X) for better capturing in the poor quality FFPE.
The coding regions (CDS) of BRCA1/2 and other HRR genes were selected based on latest MANE (Matched Annotation from NCBI and EBI) and GENCODE gene models.
Our design also covered 20 bases upstream and downstream of the exon-intron boundaries for the identification of splice site disease causing variants.
Approximately 50-100 ng of DNA was used for targeted library preparation using a custom hybrid capture kit (Twist Library Prep Kit EF with AMP Mix cat#101058 Twist Bioscience, USA).
Library quality was checked using a Qubit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) and TapeStation (Agilent, USA).
Libraries that met the quality standards were quantified, loaded at a concentration of 120 pM, and sequenced as 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads on an Illumina Novaseq X plus.

The sequencing process adhered to the manufacturer's protocol, employing the NovaSeq X Series 25B Reagent Kit 300Cyc (Cat No. 20104706), and achieved an average sequencing depth of approximately 250x for the analysis of somatic mutations.
The sequencing data undergoes an optimized workflow to determine the HRD status.
Initially, this workflow assesses the quality of the reads and trims them as needed.
After trimming, the reads were aligned to the hg38 reference genome and collapsed based on Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) information to generate a consensus BAM file.
Variant calling was then performed on this consensus BAM file for all targeted regions of HRR genes.
Deleterious mutations were identified using a well-established mutation prioritization process and annotated with the comprehensive mutation annotation tool, VariMAT.
This tool annotates mutations across various population and disease databases.

This assay evaluates the HRD status using a combined approach based on the genome aberration (GA) score, which is a quantitative measure of genomic alterations derived from high-quality ~46K SNP markers and clinically significant variants from the BRCA1/2 gene.
This assay identifies high-quality SNVs, InDels, and splice site mutations and estimates allelespecific copy numbers based on their bi-allele frequency and coverage.
The GA score (GAS) was calculated by considering different levels of copy number changes with a positivity threshold of ≥40.
A sample is classified as HRD-positive if P/LP variants were detected in the BRCA1/2 genes and/or the GAS ≥40.
Additionally, this assay determines the copy number status of CCNE1, which was considered amplified if its copy number was ≥7.
In the evaluation of HRD in ovarian cancer, current evidence suggests that only pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in the BRCA1/2 genes hold clinical significance.

Consequently, although the SOPHiA and MG_HRD assays include multiple genes in the homologous recombination repair (HRR) panel, this study focused exclusively on BRCA1/2 variants for HRD interpretation.

The identified somatic BRCA1/2 variants were classified according to the ASCO-CAP and AMP guidelines, categorizing them as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or variants of uncertain significance (VUS) 17 .
text.formatted: The identified somatic BRCA1/2 variants were classified according to the ASCO-CAP and AMP guidelines, categorizing them as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or variants of uncertain significance (VUS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: Nonsense, frameshift insertions/deletions, in-frame and canonical splice site variants classified as P/LP were grouped as pathogenic.

These pathogenic variants were further verified using the ClinVar, Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD) and BRCA Exchange databases, and only clinically significant variants were considered for downstream HRD status analyses.
Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in BRCA1/2 genes were classified as negative for BRCA status within this HRD assessment framework.
In this study, we did not conduct germline testing; therefore, the BRCA1/2 mutations identified could be of either germline or somatic origin.
Mutations in BRCA1/2 with a variant allele frequency (VAF) exceeding 40% were considered to infer the probability of germline origin.

text.text: A total of 4163 FFPE OC samples from both prevalence and validation cohorts were retrospectively analyzed using three HRD testing platforms: AmoyDx (n = 1097), SOPHiA (n = 470), and MG_HRD (n = 2596).
The clinicopathological characteristics of the total cases are summarized in Table 1.

text.text: The median age at diagnosis was 55 years, and the mean age was 54.6 years.
The cohort predominantly comprised patients with FIGO stage III disease (53.5%), followed by stage II (36.2%).
High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) was the most frequently represented histological subtype (82.5%).
Most FFPE specimens were obtained from primary tumor sites (76.4%), while 23.6% were derived from metastatic sites, primarily pelvic lymph nodes and peritoneal nodules, followed by liver.
To evaluate analytical performance, the MG_HRD assay was validated using reference standards and clinical samples with known HRD status of AmoyDx [n=157] and SOPHiA [n=13] assays.

Higher concordance was observed between AmoyDx/SOPHiA and MG_HRD assays for these 170 OC samples, yielding 96.39% Positive Percentage Agreement (PPA), 98.3% Negative Percent Agreement (NPA), and 97.05% Overall Percent Agreement (OPA).
Of the 170 samples, 165 had the same HRD status, whereas only five were discordant.
Among these five discordant cases, all were concordant with BRCA1/2_wt results, while only discordant at HRD_GS values.
Four out of five samples were HRD_GS-positive by AmoyDx (GSS ≥50) but HRD_GS-negative by MG_HRD (GAS <40), whereas one sample showed the reverse result.

Using FFPE samples, the assay was evaluated across a range of tumor content proportions (10-90%).

The MG_HRD assay results demonstrated 100% concordance across all testing conditions, indicating excellent reproducibility and robustness.
Analysis of QC metrics revealed overall a good sequencing performance for all the three different assays.
In the AmoyDx cohort, median alignment rate was 98.9% (IQR: 98.6-99.2%) and median effective depth of BRCA and SNP was 2498× and 472× respectively.
The SOPHiA cohort achieved the high target coverage with a median BRCA coverage and panel coverage percentile of 100% and 99.9%, respectively.

Despite differences in platformspecific QC metrics and sequencing designs, all assays consistently indicated greater coverage and robust sequencing quality for both BRCA and HRD analysis.

text.text: HRD testing in ovarian cancer has emerged as a crucial predictive biomarker, particularly for guiding therapeutic strategies involving PARP inhibitors.

The FDA-approved CDx Myriad myChoice test is frequently employed for this purpose; however, for Indian patients it is costly, necessitates stringent quality standards, and involves prolonged result turnaround times, thereby limiting accessibility for patients 6, 25 .
text.formatted: The FDA-approved CDx Myriad myChoice test is frequently employed for this purpose; however, for Indian patients it is costly, necessitates stringent quality standards, and involves prolonged result turnaround times, thereby limiting accessibility for patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25</ref> .

text.text: Therefore, the development of more affordable and reliable in-house HRD assays are needed, which can be implemented in standard molecular laboratories that could enhance patient access, reduce costs, and expedite treatment decision-making.
Various studies have described laboratory-developed HRD assays using different gene panels, HRD score thresholds, bioinformatic pipelines, and sequencing platforms 3, 13 .
text.formatted: Various studies have described laboratory-developed HRD assays using different gene panels, HRD score thresholds, bioinformatic pipelines, and sequencing platforms <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: Consistent with this, the recent AMP/ACCC/CAP joint consensus recommendations identified substantial heterogeneity in current commercial and laboratorydeveloped HRD assays regarding biomarker selection, scoring methods, validation strategies, and reporting practices 26 .
text.formatted: Consistent with this, the recent AMP/ACCC/CAP joint consensus recommendations identified substantial heterogeneity in current commercial and laboratorydeveloped HRD assays regarding biomarker selection, scoring methods, validation strategies, and reporting practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26</ref> .

text.text: These findings emphasize the need for rigorously validated and standardized in-house HRD assays to facilitate reliable clinical implementation and broader adoption in routine practice.
In this retrospective study, we present our experience of implementing an in-house developed HRD testing in our diagnostic laboratory.

We assessed the feasibility, reliability and reproducibility of our MG_HRD assay by comparing results from the commercially available diagnostic assays [AmoyDx and SOPHiA] along with the reference assay, Myriad MyChoice CDx.

We observed that the MG_HRD assay showed a complete concordance (100%) rate of HRD status with the AmoyDx assay among four samples and the outsourced Myriad myChoice CDx assay among five samples, which is similar to the reported studies 12, 27 .
text.formatted: We observed that the MG_HRD assay showed a complete concordance (100%) rate of HRD status with the AmoyDx assay among four samples and the outsourced Myriad myChoice CDx assay among five samples, which is similar to the reported studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27</ref> .

text.text: High concordance was observed for HRD_GS status, BRCA1/2 mutation status, and overall HRD classification, defined by the combined assessment of HRD_GS and BRCA1/2 alterations.
This result demonstrates that the MG_HRD assay can be used as a reliable and potentially more accessible alternative to the Myriad myChoice CDx for HRD assessment in ovarian cancer patients.
Previous studies have demonstrated a high level of agreement between different HRD assays and the Myriad assay.
Fumagalli C et al. reported that AmoyDx HRD Focus Panel showed an overall percent agreement (OPA) of 87.8% (65/74 tumors) compared with MyChoice CDx 3 .
Similarly, Wehn AK et al. reported an OPA of up to 96% (n=198), with a PPA of 95.2% and an NPA of 96.8% for Illumina's TruSight Oncology 500 compared to MyChoice CDx 28 .

text.text: These findings highlight the strong performance of the MG_HRD assay and its high degree of agreement with orthogonal platforms, including the AmoyDx HRD Focus and SOPHiA HRD assays, supporting its reliability for clinical implementation.
Our study indicated that the proportion of HRD-positive ovarian cancer cases ranged from 45% to 55% across the three evaluated assays.
Specifically, the percentages were 44.7% for SOPHiA, 52.8% for MG_HRD and 54.8% for AmoyDx.
These findings are consistent with previously published data.
For instance, Guarischi-Sousa et al. reported HRD positivity rates of 45.9% and 65% using SOPHiA and AmoyDx assays, respectively 6.

text.text: Similarly, Fumagalli et al. observed 48.8% HRD-positive tumors using the AmoyDx assay, while data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) indicated an approximate HRD prevalence of 50% among high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSC) cases 3, 31 .

text.text: The observed variability in HRD positivity across studies may be attributed to differences in assay methodologies and the thresholds used to define genomic instability.
The proportions of HRD_GS-positive cases identified by AmoyDx, SOPHiA, and MG_HRD assays were 47.9%, 36.6%, and 46%, respectively, in our total study cohort.
These results are slightly higher than those reported by Pepe et al. where HRD score positivity ranged between 30% to 45% for both AmoyDx and SOPHiA platforms 11 .

text.text: Additionally, Romey et al. and Denkert et al. reported GIS positivity rates of 40.5% and 38.1% using the Myriad and standardized Myriad assays, respectively 30, 32 .

text.text: Regardless of the HRD_GS status, we observed consistent frequencies of pathogenic BRCA1/2 mutations across all three assays ranging from 23.2 % -23.8% with an overall frequency of 23.6%.
This aligns closely with the 22% prevalence reported by Landen et al study 33.
text.formatted: This aligns closely with the 22% prevalence reported by Landen et al study <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">33</ref>.

text.text: Our study further revealed that tumors with BRCA1/2 mutations had significantly elevated HRD genomic scores compared to those with BRCA1/2_wt (p < 0.0001), consistent with previous reports 32, 34, 35 .

22.2 for AmoyDx, 3.0 vs. -4.1 for SOPHiA, and 57.0 vs.
28.0 for the MG_HRD assay, respectively.
Similarly, Morgan et al. and Romey et al. reported higher median GIS for Myriad assay in BRCA1/2 mutated versus wild-type tumors (62 vs. 28; p < 0.0001) 32, 34 .

text.text: The observed variation in absolute median HRD scores across the assays indicates that the HRD scores are assay-specific and should not be directly compared between the platforms.

Although these assays differ in scoring algorithms, genomic metrics, and assayspecific thresholds, they converge on the same biological concept that BRCA mutated tumors consistently harbour a higher genomic scar burden than the wild-type tumors.
A substantial proportion of tumors in our cohort were BRCA1/2_wt but HRD_GSpositive (28.8% overall), with frequencies ranging from 20.9% with SOPHiA, 31.6% with AmoyDx, and 29.0% with MG_HRD.

This distribution is broadly consistent with previous studies, including 30% reported by Yuan et al 36 using AmoyDx, 23% by Rojo et al 37 using SOPHiA, 26.2% by Romey et al 32 using Myriad, and 30.2% by Denkert et al 30 using a standardized Myriad HRD assay.

text.text: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the frequency of this molecular subgroup of our MG_HRD assay is on par with the Myriad assay 32 .

text.text: This observation highlights that a considerable subset of patients with HRD_GS positivity would be missed by BRCA testing alone, yet they could potentially benefit from treatment with PARPi.

Comparative analysis of BRCA1/2 mutation spectra revealed a consistent predominance of truncating variants in both genes, indicating that loss-of-function is the primary mechanism of gene inactivation.

Several recurrent variants were identified in the BRCA1/2 genes; among these, the BRCA1 c.68_69del (p.Glu23ValfsTer17) variant was the most prevalent pathogenic variant, with a frequency of 14% [97/693] detected in ovarian cancer.
This hotspot mutation is also known as "185delAG" and commonly known as the "Ashkenazi Jewish population founder mutation".
This variant has also been widely reported across diverse Asian populations 38 , including the Indian population in breast and ovarian carcinoma cases.
text.formatted: This variant has also been widely reported across diverse Asian populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">38</ref> , including the Indian population in breast and ovarian carcinoma cases.

text.text: Singh et al. reported this germline variant in 3.4% (34/1,010) of patients with breast and ovarian cancer, while John et al. reported it in 24.5% of all pathogenic BRCA1 variants [29/181] in a cohort of 921 breast and ovarian cancer cases through germline testing 39,40 .
Likewise, Parween et al. observed this variant in 7.2% (8/110) of pathogenic BRCA1 variants among patients with gynaecologic cancers, encompassing both somatic and germline tests 41 .
text.formatted: Likewise, Parween et al. observed this variant in 7.2% (8/110) of pathogenic BRCA1 variants among patients with gynaecologic cancers, encompassing both somatic and germline tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">41</ref> .

text.text: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to report the BRCA1 c.68_69del mutation exclusively in Indian patients with ovarian carcinoma using somatic BRCA testing methods.
Collectively, these findings reinforce the prevalence of the BRCA1 c.
68_69del variant in the Indian population and highlight its clinical significance as an important target for routine BRCA testing and genetic risk assessment.
Tumor cellularity is an important pre-analytical factor that can influence HRD assessment.
Although a TC of approximately 30% is generally preferable for a reliable analysis, HRD testing has also been successfully performed in samples with lower TC.
Romey et al.
reported successful HRD analysis in 61.8% (264/427) of samples with TC<30% 32.

text.text: Furthermore, several clinically validated assays, including FoundationOne® CDx 42 , Caris HRD, SeqOne HRD solution, and CancerPrecision® (CeGaT), permit testing in samples with TC as low as 20% 10 .

text.text: This finding suggests that TC may influence HRD detection while supporting the feasibility of HRD assessment in specimens with TC ≥20%.
These observations are particularly relevant in real-world settings, where limited tumor material and variable tumor cellularity may otherwise restrict access to HRD testing.
HGSC was the predominant subtype in our cohort, with a significantly higher frequency than non-HGSC, consistent with prior reports.
Overall, 82.5% of cases were HGSC, of which 60.2% were HRD-positive, aligning with studies demonstrating the strong association of HRD with HGSC 43 .
text.formatted: Overall, 82.5% of cases were HGSC, of which 60.2% were HRD-positive, aligning with studies demonstrating the strong association of HRD with HGSC <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">43</ref> .

text.text: Although in our study HRD was enriched in HGSC, it was also observed across non-HGSC subtypes.
In low-grade serous carcinoma, we detected lower HRD positivity [3.8%] compared to 15% reported by Cunningham et al 44 .
text.formatted: In low-grade serous carcinoma, we detected lower HRD positivity [3.8%] compared to 15% reported by Cunningham et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">44</ref> .

text.text: In clear cell carcinoma, HRD prevalence varied widely across studies, with 28% reported by Cunningham et al., 2.3% by Liu et al., while our study showed an intermediate rate of 13.7% (16/117) 44,45 .
Carcinosarcoma exhibited a higher HRD frequency in our cohort (52.9%, 9/17) compared with the 25% reported by Denkert et al.

This difference may reflect methodological variations between the studies, as our HRD classification incorporated both pathogenic BRCA mutations and genomic scar positivity, whereas Denkert et al. defined HRD positivity based on only the genomic instability score 30 .

text.text: Similarly, the endometrioid carcinoma showed a higher HRD prevalence in our study (26.7%, 35/131) compared to 19% [5/26] reported by Pierson et al 46 .

text.text: In contrast, mucinous carcinoma demonstrated a very low HRD positivity (2.2%), but no supporting evidence was found.

Therefore, the presence of HRD in these less common histological subtypes underscores the importance of HRD profiling across these ovarian cancer subtypes, especially when they exhaust their standard therapeutic options.

Future studies should focus on prospective multicenter cohorts to validate the clinical utility of HRD testing.
Further studies are needed to analyze treatment responses with longitudinal follow-up.
The observation of HRD positivity in cases other than HGSC, such as carcinosarcoma and CCC, underscores the importance of non-HGOC cases for future investigations.

Further exploration of resistance mechanisms, including BRCA reversion mutations and CCNE1 amplification, may facilitate the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies for patients with OC. .
Conclusions This is the first Indian study to develop, validate, and implement an in-house HRD assay in a diagnostic laboratory.
The present data evaluated across three different HRD assays enabled the assessment of HRD and BRCA prevalence in a large real-world ovarian cancer cohort.
Our findings indicate that the MG_HRD assay is technically feasible, diagnostically reliable, and reproducible.

The high level of agreement observed across platforms, including strong concordance, underscores the robustness of the MG_HRD assay as a cost-effective, flexible alternative to commercial solutions, thereby enhancing accessibility in Indian clinical settings.

The findings of this study offer valuable support to clinicians and diagnostic laboratories, highlighting the use of the MG_HRD assay for assessing HRD, which can significantly benefit patients with ovarian cancer undergoing PARPi therapy, especially in lower-and middle-income countries.
